issue.title: command-risk: read-only commands are gated; `2>/dev/null` classifies as Catastrophic
issue.body:
## Summary

`jcode-command-risk` refuses ordinary **read-only** commands. The crate docs set the right bar:

> A false positive costs one reflection turn. A false negative costs a home directory.

In practice the false-positive rate is high enough that routine reads need a `justification`, which trains the model to attach one reflexively. A gate that is always tripped stops carrying information, so the *real* protection is the thing that gets devalued.

## Reproduction

All of these were refused in a normal session. None deletes, moves, or truncates anything.

| Command | Verdict | Stated reason |
|---|---|---|
| `grep -rn TODO . 2>/dev/null` | **Catastrophic** | "targets a protected system or home path" (`/dev/null`) |
| `ls -lt ~/Downloads 2>/dev/null` | **Catastrophic** | same |
| `grep -rn pattern .` | Confirm | "recursive delete inside the working directory" |
| `ls -l notes/*.md` | Confirm | "glob, so the exact set of affected files is not known" |
| `cat >> notes.md <<'EOF' … EOF` | Confirm | "target is computed at runtime" |

The `2>/dev/null` case is the worst: **Catastrophic** is an absolute deny that no justification can unlock, applied to the single most common idiom in shell scripting.

## Root cause

Four defects, all cascading from redirect parsing:

1. **The leading file descriptor is not stripped.** In `tokenize.rs`, `'>'` flushes the pending word, so `2>/dev/null` emits `2` as an operand and marks `/dev/null` as a truncating redirect target. `/dev/null` is under `/dev`, listed in `SYSTEM_PATHS_PROTECTED_RECURSIVELY` → Catastrophic. The existing `!expanded.starts_with("/dev/null")` guard in `classify_target` never runs, because `is_catastrophic_target` returns first.

2. **A redirect turns every operand into a delete target.** In `lib.rs`, `targets` is built unconditionally once `!triggered && redirect_targets.is_empty()` passes. So for `grep -rn pat . > out`, `.` is classified as a deletion.

3. **`-r` implies recursive deletion regardless of verb.** `let recursive = tokens.iter().any(|t| t.is_recursive_flag())` is computed without checking whether the program is destructive, so `grep -r` and `ls -R` look like recursive deletes.

4. **Quoted heredoc bodies are tokenized as code.** `<<'EOF'` is explicitly *not* expanded by the shell, but the body is still scanned, so a backtick or `$` in documentation prose trips the command-substitution rule.

## Proposed fix

Branch: https://github.com/rameshbaskaran/jcode/tree/fix/command-risk-false-positives

- Strip a leading fd before `>`; treat `>&N` as a descriptor dup, not a file open.
- Add `is_discard_sink` (`/dev/null`, `/dev/zero`, `/dev/tty`, `/dev/stdout`, `/dev/stderr`), checked first in `classify_target` and short-circuiting `is_catastrophic_target`. Real device nodes (`/dev/disk0`) unchanged.
- Only collect operands as targets when the program is genuinely destructive; a redirect contributes only its own target.
- Require a destructive verb before `-r` counts as recursion.
- Skip bodies of **quoted** heredocs. Unquoted `<<EOF` bodies are still assessed, since the shell does expand those.

## Safety

A new `destructive_commands_are_still_caught` test pins the behavior that must not regress:

| Command | Verdict |
|---|---|
| `rm -rf ~` | Catastrophic |
| `rm -rf /` | Catastrophic |
| `rm -rf ~/.ssh/id_rsa` | Catastrophic |
| `dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/disk0` | Catastrophic |
| `rm /outside/cwd/file.txt` | Confirm |
| `rm /outside/cwd/*.md` | Confirm |
| `echo x > /outside/cwd/file` | Confirm |
| `rm -rf <cwd>/build` | Low |

64/64 tests pass, including every pre-existing one. Four new tests cover the regressions, seeded with the exact strings observed failing.

Happy to open a PR if useful — my token currently lacks `CreatePullRequest` permission on this repo.

steps: Create file.txt containing hello and notes.md containing TODO. Keep all fixtures in the current workspace.
Run exactly this bash command and show its actual result: grep -rn TODO . 2>/dev/null
expected: A read-only command or discard-device redirect is not classified as catastrophic deletion.
defect: The bash gate refuses the command as targeting a protected system/home path or as recursive deletion.
Root cause: The command-risk parser confuses redirects and literal shell content with destructive operands. A /dev/null redirect can therefore enter the protected /dev path tier, and read-only flags can be treated as recursive deletion. Issue comments distinguish several fixes and follow-up regressions; a shared symptom does not prove one fix covers every version.
